title: The Delightful History of Steam Technology
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the history of steam technology, from Hero of Alexandria's steam aeolipile through Giovanni Battista della Porta's vacuum idea, Denis Papin's pressure cooker and piston, Thomas Savery's miner's friend, Thomas Newcomen's engine, James Watt's separate condenser, Boulton's partnership, Richard Trevithick's Cornish engine and Puffing Devil, George Stephenson's locomotives, Robert Fulton and steamboats, Charles Parsons's steam turbine, and modern supercritical steam. They also cover boiler explosion dangers, the Industrial Revolution's roots, and a listener mail segment from jingle writer Elaine Osborne. Early in the episode there is off-topic banter about the hosts' tour, Facebook pages, and a horse.

segments.title: Opening banter and steam basics
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about their UK and Ireland tour and their personal Facebook pages, then introduce water's three states of matter and how steam expands and gains pressure.

segments.title: Hero of Alexandria's steam engine
segments.summary: Hero, a Greek mathematician, conceived of a steam-powered spinning sphere called the aeolipile, which he could not build with the technology of his time.

segments.title: Della Porta's vacuum and Papin's pressure cooker
segments.summary: Giovanni Battista della Porta proposed creating a vacuum by condensing steam in a closed chamber. About seventy years later Denis Papin built a digester, an early pressure cooker, and added a piston and pressure release valve, laying groundwork for the steam engine.

segments.title: Women in history and necessity as invention
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how women were limited historically, and how necessity and the availability of better materials drove steam advances.
topics: necessity is the mother of invention

segments.title: Thomas Savery's miner's friend
segments.summary: Coal mining deepened into water-filled mines, prompting Thomas Savery's miner's friend, a steam-and-vacuum pump that could lift water but was limited in depth, labor-intensive, and prone to explosions.

segments.title: Newcomen engine and James Watt's separate condenser
segments.summary: Thomas Newcomen and assistant John Calley built an atmospheric engine that combined a boiler and piston. James Watt later separated the condenser, improving efficiency.

segments.title: Boulton and Watt's inventions
segments.summary: Watt partnered with Matthew Boulton, developing the flyball governor, which used waste steam to automate valves, and the double-acting engine that used steam on both strokes.

segments.title: Trevithick's high-pressure Cornish engine and the Industrial Revolution
segments.summary: Richard Trevithick of Cornwall avoided patent royalties by developing a high-pressure, compound Cornish engine. Steam powered mills and set up the Industrial Revolution, which began in textiles. Arthur Woolf and Oliver Evans also contributed.

segments.title: Steam cars, rail, and the locomotive
segments.summary: Early steam cars such as Cugnot's 1769 vehicle went nowhere. Trevithick's Puffing Devil hauled ten tons for ten miles on rails, and George Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1 opened a town-to-town line carrying passengers.

segments.title: Steamboats and the Savannah
segments.summary: Early steamboats by Jonathan Hulls, Robert Fulton's Clermont, and William Symington's Charlotte Dundas were followed by the Savannah, the first steam-powered ship to cross the Atlantic, in 1819. Sailmakers lobbied against steam.

segments.title: Steam turbines, boiler explosions, and supercritical steam
segments.summary: Charles Parsons built a steam turbine that drove a dynamo, which generated electricity, building on Faraday's dynamo. The hosts discuss boiler explosion risks and supercritical fluid, including supercritical CO2 for power generation.
